event.description:
Cooper’s Is Closed in observance of Memorial Day.

Closed on Memorial Day

As we take a moment to honor and remember the brave men and women who made the ultimate sacrifice while serving our country, we would like to inform you that we will be closed on Memorial Day, [specific date].

Memorial Day is a day of reflection and remembrance, a time to pay tribute to those who selflessly dedicated their lives to protect our freedom. It is a day to gather with loved ones, visit memorials, and participate in ceremonies that commemorate the sacrifices of our fallen heroes.

❤️ At Cooper’s Seafood House, we hold deep respect for the significance of Memorial Day. We believe it is important to observe this day with solemnity and gratitude. Therefore, our doors will be closed on this day to allow our staff and customers to participate in honoring the memory of our servicemen and servicewomen.

⏰ We will resume our regular business hours on [next business day]. We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause and appreciate your understanding as we join the nation in paying tribute to our fallen heroes.

On this Memorial Day, we encourage you to take a moment to reflect, express gratitude, and honor the memory of those who made the ultimate sacrifice. Let us come together as a community to remember their bravery, their courage, and their unwavering commitment to our country.

Memorial Day, originally called Decoration Day, is a day of remembrance for those who have died in service of the United States of America. Over two dozen cities and towns claim to be the birthplace of Memorial Day. While Waterloo N.Y. was officially declared the birthplace of Memorial Day by President Lyndon Johnson in May 1966, it’s difficult to prove conclusively the origins of the day.

Regardless of the exact date or location of its origins, one thing is clear – Memorial Day was borne out of the Civil War and a desire to honor our dead. It was officially proclaimed on 5 May 1868 by General John Logan, national commander of the Grand Army of the Republic, in his General Order No. 11. “The 30th of May, 1868, is designated for the purpose of strewing with flowers, or otherwise decorating the graves of comrades who died in defense of their country during the late rebellion, and whose bodies now lie in almost every city, village and hamlet churchyard in the land,” he proclaimed. The date of Decoration Day, as he called it, was chosen because it wasn’t the anniversary of any particular battle.

On the first Decoration Day, General James Garfield made a speech at Arlington National Cemetery, and 5,000 participants decorated the graves of the 20,000 Union and Confederate soldiers buried there.

The first state to officially recognize the holiday was New York in 1873. By 1890 it was recognized by all of the northern states. The South refused to acknowledge the day, honoring their dead on separate days until after World War I (when the holiday changed from honoring just those who died fighting in the Civil War to honoring Americans who died fighting in any war).

It is now observed in almost every state on the last Monday in May with Congressional passage of the National Holiday Act of 1971 (P.L. 90 – 363). This helped ensure a three day weekend for Federal holidays, though several southern states have an additional separate day for honoring the Confederate war dead: January 19th in Texas; April 26th in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, and Mississippi; May 10th in South Carolina; and June 3rd (Jefferson Davis’ birthday) in Louisiana and Tennessee.

History After Dark: Ghost Hunt at the John Jay French Museum

Do you believe in ghosts? Join the Beaumont Heritage Society and our partners at Ghost Texas for History After Dark, an after-hours paranormal investigation experience at one of Beaumont’s most storied historic properties — the John Jay French Museum.

Ghost Texas, a professional paranormal investigation group based in Houston, Texas, will lead participants through the museum after dark, exploring its history and the mysteries that may still linger within its walls. Whether you’re a seasoned ghost hunter or a curious first-timer, this is your chance to investigate the unknown for yourself.

Your ticket purchase directly supports the care and maintenance of the John Jay French Museum, helping preserve this irreplaceable piece of Beaumont’s history for generations to come.

Event Details

📅 October 9–10, 2026
📍 John Jay French Museum, Beaumont, TX
🎟️ $60 per person | Beaumont Heritage Society members receive a discount — check your email for your exclusive code!

Session 2: 9:30 PM – 11:30 PM

Saturday, October 10th:

Session 1: 7:00 PM – 9:00 PM (SOLD OUT)
Session 2: 9:30 PM – 11:30 PM

 

What to Know Before You Go

  • Participants must be 16 years of age or older
  • All participants must sign a liability waiver upon arrival
  • Please arrive 15 minutes before your selected session time
  • Dress comfortably — you’ll be on your feet and moving through the museum
  • Ghost Texas will have professional equipment on-site
  • Personal photography and video are welcome — no flash photography inside the museum, please
  • Guests may not live stream the event; Ghost Texas and the Beaumont Heritage Society reserve the right to ask guests not to film or photograph certain areas or moments

Tickets are limited to 20 participants per session — don’t wait to grab yours!

 

Traveling to Beaumont? Stay in our host hotel!

event.venue_json: {"id":2301,"global_id":"mcfaddin-ward.org?id=2301","venue":"McFaddin-Ward House Visitor Center","address":"1906 Calder","city":"Beaumont","country":"United States","state":"TX","zip":"77701","website":"www.mcfaddin-ward.org","phone":"409-832-1906","url":"https://mcfaddin-ward.org/venue/mcfaddin-ward-house-visitor-center/","show_map":true,"show_map_link":true}
event.description:
Join the McFaddin-Ward House Museum for “America 250: A Beaumont History,” a free public lecture presented by Judith Walker Linsley on Thursday, November 12, at 6:30 p.m. in the Museum’s Visitor Center Lecture Hall (1906 Calder Avenue, Beaumont).

In commemoration of America’s 250th anniversary, Linsley, a sixth-generation Southeast Texan and local historian, will explore the fascinating story of Beaumont, beginning with the Indigenous Ishak people and traveling through the Texas Revolution, the 1901 Spindletop oil boom, and technological and industrial expansions leading up to the modern day.

For nearly four decades, Linsley has been a member of the McFaddin-Ward House Museum staff, serving in a range of roles in interpretation, education, curation, and research, including her current role as research assistant. She has also conducted more than 100 oral history interviews for the Museum.

A Lamar University alumna with a Bachelor of Arts in Spanish and a Master of Arts in History, Linsley served as the second director of Lamar’s Center for History and Culture of Southeast Texas and the Upper Gulf Coast and has been an adjunct instructor of both Texas and U.S. history at Lamar.

She has co-authored three books, including the award-winning Giant Under the Hill: A History of the Spindletop Oil Discovery at Beaumont, Texas, in 1901 (2002) and The McFaddin-Ward House (1992), and numerous historical articles.

McFaddin-Ward House Museum lectures are admission-free and open to the public, but space is limited. Doors open at 6 p.m. For more information, call 409-832-2134.

For those unable to attend, the full lecture will be available for viewing on the Museum YouTube Channel (youtube.com/@mcfaddinwardhouse), Facebook (facebook.com/McFaddinWardHouse), and website (mcfaddin-ward.org/about/videos) after the event.

The lecture is part of Southeast Texas 250, a regional initiative to commemorate the U.S. Semiquincentennial celebration. Led by the Beaumont Heritage Society, Southeast Texas 250 brings together museums, historical organizations, schools, civic groups, and local governments throughout the region to celebrate the people, places, and stories that have shaped Southeast Texas and its role in the broader American story.

event.description:
Join Rhythm of Our Roots, a free intergenerational community gathering presented by The Healing Portal Collective that transforms the park into a space for wellness, creativity, and connection. Experience guided Meridian Movement with Dr. Charlie Trinh, exploring gentle stretching, breathwork, and mindful movement inspired by Traditional Chinese Medicine. Relax into a restorative crystal bowl sound journey led by Blossom Legend, then join our signature community drum circle facilitated by Meesh Martinez, where rhythm becomes a shared language that brings people together.

Designed for all ages and experience levels, this gathering offers accessible practices that support emotional well-being, self-expression, and community connection. Come as you are and rediscover the rhythm that connects us all.

Presented as part of Buffalo Bayou Partnership’s Park Partners program, an initiative that connects neighborhood organizations with opportunities to activate parks, trails, and unique spaces along Buffalo Bayou.

Cost
Free

Duration
12-5 PM

Meeting Location
Garver Park (705 Lockwood Dr)

FREE REGISTRATION

 

Meet the Team

Dr. Charlie Trinh / Trinhquility is a Doctor of Acupuncture and Chinese Medicine, holistic healer, and community wellness advocate based in Houston. With a unique background in engineering and a deep-rooted calling toward Eastern medicine, Dr. Trinh integrates Traditional Chinese Medicine, movement practices, and energetic healing to support the body’s natural ability to restore balance. His work bridges ancient wisdom with modern understanding, emphasizing the connection between physical health, emotional well-being, and the surrounding environment. Through his practice, Trinhquility, Dr. Trinh has developed Meridian Movements, a mindful movement system designed to activate the body’s energetic pathways, improve circulation, and reconnect individuals to their natural rhythms. His vision for the Bayou project is to bring accessible, community-centered healing into nature, creating spaces where individuals can engage in intentional movement, breath, and awareness alongside the living ecosystem. By aligning human health with environmental harmony, Dr. Trinh aims to foster resilience, connection, and collective well-being within the Houston community.

Meesh Martinez / Primitive Experience is a multimedia producer, filmmaker, and community arts facilitator based in Houston, Texas. An Austin native who grew up in Mexico City, Meesh holds a Bachelor’s degree in Cinematographic Language, a background that informs his work in visual storytelling, cultural documentation, and multimedia production. In Houston, Meesh collaborates with artists, organizations, and cultural institutions to produce video, photography, and digital media that document performances, community initiatives, and creative projects. His work focuses on amplifying cultural expression and strengthening connections between artists and communities. Meesh is also the founder of Primitive Experience, an initiative that creates immersive gatherings through drum circles, music, movement, and nature-based practices designed to foster connection, creativity, and collective well-being. Meesh is certified in facilitating drum circles for emotional regulation, using rhythm and group participation as tools for personal and community healing. In addition to his artistic and multimedia work, Meesh contributes to youth development programs and will be participating in the leadership and direction team for Peace Camp, supporting programming that nurtures creativity, emotional awareness, and community values for young participants. Meesh is also currently leading projects supported through grant funding that expand access to participatory arts experiences and cultural programming in Houston.

Blossom Legend / Goddess Glow Birthing is a full-spectrum community doula, herbalist, chef, musician, and wellness facilitator dedicated to creating experiences that nourish the body, mind, and spirit. With more than a decade of experience in community wellness, culinary arts, and holistic care, her work weaves together ancestral wisdom, cultural traditions, nourishment, sound, and collective healing. Rooted in Afro-Caribbean traditions and a deep commitment to community care, Blossom creates spaces where people can slow down, reconnect with themselves, and experience healing in ways that are both accessible and transformative. As a chef of over twelve years, Blossom believes food is one of our most powerful medicines and a pathway to connection. Her culinary work focuses on nourishing meals, herbal preparations, botanical beverages, and community-centered dining experiences that celebrate the relationship between wellness, culture, and the earth. As an herbalist and doula, she supports individuals and families through life’s transitions, offering holistic care that honors the physical, emotional, and spiritual dimensions of well-being. At Rhythm of Our Roots, Blossom will guide a restorative sound bath experience designed to help participants release stress, regulate the nervous system, and reconnect with their own inner rhythm. Using healing vibrations, frequency harmonics, and meditative soundscapes, she invites participants into a state of deep rest, reflection, and renewal. Her approach is grounded in the belief that personal healing ripples outward, strengthening families, communities, and future generations.
